newsitem.title: GERMANY: German state to probe employees over Scientology.
newsitem.headline: German state to probe employees over Scientology.

text.p: The southern German state of Bavaria said on Tuesday it would require all state employees to fill out a questionnaire detailing their ties to the Church of Scientology.

The state chancellery said applicants for state jobs, including teachers and police officers, would not be hired if they refused to fill out the questionnaire. Those already employed would face disciniplary measures if they declined.
The move was immediately criticised by the Church of Scientology, which said the Bavarian decree was unconstitutional.

"This is naturally illegal and we will take appropriate action," said Sabine Weber, a spokeswoman for the Scientologists in Germany. "It violates the constitution to ask people about their religious beliefs before hiring them."
The Bavarian government has been at the forefront of efforts in Germany designed to place limits on the Scientologists.
Leaders of Germany's 16 regional states said last week they would consider whether the Church of Scientology should be put under surveillance by the government's anti-extremist watchdog.
Bavaria also urged the states to consider enacting a nationwide ban on Scientology members from public service.
Weber said that Bavaria was ignoring international criticism of Germany for its treatment of Scientologists.
"This shows that Bavaria hasn't learned anything from the recent past," she said. "It also shows that Germany hasn't learned about discrimination from its history."

The Bavarian decree also requires any private companies awarded state contracts in certain sensitive fields to sign a statement saying they will not use the methods of Scientology founder L. Ron Hubbard.
Bavaria said the measures were designed to "prevent Scientologists from infiltrating public positions".
Scientology says it has around 30,000 German members. The government puts the figure between 10,000 and 20,000.
